formNote: This pattern turns a verb into a noun with 기 and then feeds it to 시작하다 (始作하다, Sino-Korean 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do'), so literally you are 'doing the beginning of the action'. Use it when you want to spotlight the very moment an action gets underway: 비가 오기 시작했어요 ('it started to rain'). The close rival is plain 시작하다 with a noun object, 공부를 시작하다 ('start studying'): use that when the activity is already a noun, but use V기 시작하다 when you have a verb and want to keep its verb meaning. English speakers carry over 'start to' versus 'start -ing' as if Korean had two forms, but Korean only has this one, so do not say 오게 시작하다 or 와서 시작하다. The other trap is attaching 기 to a noun: 비기 시작하다 is wrong because 비 is already a noun; you need a verb stem like 오- before 기.
usage: past 했어요 is the default; the start already happened
weather verbs like 오다 take this pattern naturally
marks a true first time, a milestone
Once I start exercising I feel good.
stack 면 on the whole pattern for 'once you start'
examples: 언제 + past asks for the starting point
These days I've started reading books.
요즘 frames a newly begun habit
mistakes: Saying 비기 시작하다 — you cannot bolt 기 onto a noun. 비 is the noun 'rain'; you need the verb stem 오- first, so it is 비가 오기 시작하다.
Translating 'start to rain' as 오게 시작하다 or 와서 시작하다 by copying English 'start to' / 'start and'. Korean only nominalizes with 기 here: 오기 시작하다.
Forcing the present 시작해요 for an event that already began. Koreans default to 시작했어요 because the onset is in the past; present is mostly for narration or general statements.

formNote: V게 되다 frames a result as something that happened TO you rather than something you chose: 되다 means 'become', so the whole thing says 'it came to be that...'. Reach for it when outside circumstances, fate, or other people produced the outcome — 한국에 살게 됐어요 quietly signals 'it worked out that I live in Korea', softer and more humble than 한국에 살아요 ('I live in Korea', a flat fact). Contrast it sharply with V기로 하다, which marks a firm personal decision: 회사를 그만두기로 했어요 = 'I decided to quit' (my will), whereas 회사를 그만두게 됐어요 = 'I ended up quitting' (circumstances pushed me). Koreans love this pattern precisely because it downplays personal agency, which sounds modest and polite. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing it for plain decisions — if you clearly chose something, 게 되다 sounds evasive, as if you are dodging responsibility. Also note the spelling: 되다 contracts to 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요, in casual and polite speech.
usage: I ended up living in Korea.
result of circumstances, not a stated choice
I came to like that person.
a gradual, unplanned change of feeling
I ended up quitting the company.
implies it was not fully my decision
I've come to eat spicy food now.
이제 + pattern shows a new state you grew into
examples: How did you come to learn Korean?
어떻게...게 됐어요 politely asks 'what led you to'
I ended up taking on that task.
softens that the job was handed to you
mistakes: Using it for a clear choice, e.g. 유학 가게 됐어요 when you actively decided to study abroad. For a real decision say 유학 가기로 했어요; 게 되다 implies circumstances chose for you.
Writing 돼 as 되 (or 돼요 as 되요). The casual/polite forms are 게 돼 / 게 돼요 because 되 + 어 contracts to 돼; the bare 되 only appears before consonants like 게 됩니다.
Adding a 'by someone' agent and treating it as a passive. 게 되다 is not 'be made to'; it just states an outcome. To say someone forced you, use a causative like 그만두게 만들었어요.

formNote: V아/어 있다 describes the lingering STATE left behind after an action finishes: the door was opened and stays open, so 문이 열려 있어요 ('the door is open'). Pick 아 있다 when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다) and 어 있다 otherwise (열려 있다, 서 있다). The notorious confusion is with V고 있다, the progressive: 고 있다 is the action still happening, 아/어 있다 is the result still in place. So 앉고 있어요 = 'I am (in the act of) sitting down', while 앉아 있어요 = 'I am seated'; 문을 열고 있어요 = 'I am opening the door', 문이 열려 있어요 = 'the door is (already) open'. Notice 아/어 있다 takes mostly intransitive or passive verbs (오다, 가다, 서다, 열리다, 켜지다) and the noun gets 이/가, not 을/를. The English-speaker trap is using it with transitive action verbs like 먹다 or 읽다: 밥을 먹어 있어요 is wrong; an action you keep doing needs 고 있다 (밥을 먹고 있어요).
usage: passive 열리다 + the door takes 이/가, not 을/를
the result of turning it on still holds
I am sitting on a chair.
앉- ends in ㅏ so it takes 아 있다
a lasting state, not the act of closing
examples: The picture is hanging on the wall.
서다 → 서 있다; they remain standing
mistakes: Saying 밥을 먹어 있어요 for 'I am eating'. 먹다 is an ongoing action, not a resulting state, so it needs 고 있다: 밥을 먹고 있어요.
Marking the subject with 을/를, e.g. 문을 열려 있어요. With 아/어 있다 the thing is in a state, so it takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Mixing up 앉고 있다 and 앉아 있다. 앉고 있다 = the act of sitting down in progress; 앉아 있다 = already seated. Learners often want the second meaning but say the first.

formNote: 때 is the noun 'time/occasion', so V(으)ㄹ 때 literally means 'the time when V', naming the moment an action or state holds: 밥을 먹을 때 = 'when (I) eat'. Attach ㄹ 때 after a vowel-final stem (갈 때) and 을 때 after a consonant-final stem (먹을 때, 좋을 때). This works with adjectives too — 피곤할 때 ('when tired') — which sets it apart from time markers reserved for verbs. The key contrast is with the connective -(으)면 ('if/whenever'): -(으)ㄹ 때 pins down a specific occasion or duration ('during the time when'), while -(으)면 states a condition ('if it happens'). So 비가 올 때 우산을 써요 = 'when it rains (at that time) I use an umbrella', whereas 비가 오면 = 'if/whenever it rains'. For a completed past moment, switch to V았/었을 때: 어렸을 때 ('when I was young'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 으: consonant stems need it (좋을 때, not 좋ㄹ 때), and learners often forget that 때 is a real noun that can take particles like 에 or 부터.
usage: When I eat, I drink water.
먹- ends in a consonant, so 을 때
When I head home, I call.
가- ends in a vowel, so plain ㄹ 때
works on adjectives: 피곤하- → 피곤할 때
When I was little, I lived in Busan.
어릴 때 is a fixed phrase for childhood
examples: When I study, I listen to music.
habit that holds during the action
When the weather is nice, I take a walk.
When I was in a bad mood, I slept.
mistakes: Dropping the 으 after a consonant stem: writing 먹ㄹ 때 or 좋ㄹ 때. Consonant stems require 을 때, so it is 먹을 때, 좋을 때.
Using -(으)ㄹ 때 for a hypothetical condition where -(으)면 is needed. 비가 올 때 means 'when/at the time it rains'; for 'if it rains (then...)' use 비가 오면.
Saying 어렸을 때 as 어릴 때 (or vice versa) without minding tense. Use 어릴 때 for the general childhood period and 어렸을 때 to anchor a specific past moment.

formNote: 동안 is the noun 'a stretch of time/duration', so V는 동안 means 'during the whole time that V is going on', framing two events that share the same span: 제가 요리하는 동안 기다려 주세요 ('please wait while I cook'). Because 동안 is a present-tense duration noun, the verb takes the 는 modifier ending, never 은. Contrast it with V(으)ㄹ 때: 때 points at the moment or occasion ('at the time when'), while 동안 stresses the continuous span throughout which something runs in parallel. So 자는 동안 = 'all the while I sleep (the whole duration)', whereas 잘 때 = 'when I sleep / at sleeping time'. 동안 can also stand alone after a plain noun of duration: 방학 동안 ('during the vacation'), 한 시간 동안 ('for one hour'). The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 은 instead of 는 (자은 동안 is wrong; it must be 자는 동안), and translating 'while' too loosely — if you mean contrast ('while X, Y is different'), Korean uses -는데 or -지만, not 동안, which is purely about overlapping time.
usage: two actions run over one shared span
While I study, I keep my phone off.
main clause holds throughout the studying
It rained while I was sleeping.
a background event filling the same period
after a duration noun, 동안 stands alone
examples: While I wait, I read a book.
filling the waiting period with another act
While traveling, I took lots of photos.
an activity spread across the whole trip
While the baby slept, I cleaned.
two events overlapping in real time
mistakes: Attaching 은 to the verb: 자은 동안. 동안 is a present-duration noun, so the stem takes 는: 자는 동안.
Using 동안 to mean contrastive 'while' ('I like coffee, while she likes tea'). That is contrast, not shared time — use -는데 or -지만: 저는 커피를 좋아하는데 그 사람은 차를 좋아해요.
Forgetting that 동안 follows a bare noun directly. For 'for two hours' say 두 시간 동안, not 두 시간을 동안 or 두 시간이는 동안.

formNote: -지만 clips straight onto a verb or adjective stem to join two clauses that pull against each other: 한국어는 어렵지만 재미있어요 ('Korean is hard but fun'). It is the everyday, neutral 'but', equally at home in writing and speech. The sharp contrast to learn is -지만 versus -는데: -지만 states a clean, head-on opposition (A, but the opposite B), while -는데 gives softer background or contrast that sets up the next remark — 비싸지만 샀어요 simply says 'expensive but I bought it', whereas 비싼데 살까요? leans into 'it's pricey, so... should I buy it?'. After a noun you need the copula: 학생이지만 ('though I'm a student'), not 학생지만. Tense usually sits on the final clause, not before 지만, so 'I was tired but studied' is 피곤하지만 공부했어요, with 했 carrying the past. The English-speaker pitfall is starting a brand-new sentence with 'But...' as in English; Korean prefers to fold the contrast into one sentence with 지만, or to use 하지만/그렇지만 as a sentence-opener instead of bare 지만.
usage: contrasts two adjectives in one breath
It's raining but I'm going out.
verb stem + 지만, no tense before it
I'm hungry but I'm holding out.
sets two opposing states side by side
I'm a student, but I work too.
after a noun use 이지만, not bare 지만
examples: These clothes are pricey but pretty.
I ate a lot but I'm hungry again.
to stress the past, 었지만 is allowed
I'm tired but I study anyway.
tense stays on the second verb, 공부해요
mistakes: Forgetting the copula after a noun: 학생지만. Nouns need 이/예요's stem 이-, so it is 학생이지만 ('though a student').
Loading tense before 지만 when it belongs at the end: 갔지만 갈 거예요. Normally keep one tense on the final clause — 가지만 안 갈 거예요 is cleaner, or 갔지만 only when the first clause is truly past.
Beginning a sentence with a lone 지만 the way English starts with 'But...'. 지만 must attach to a stem; to open a sentence use 하지만 or 그렇지만.

formNote: -거나 attaches to a verb (or adjective) stem to offer alternative ACTIONS — 'do this or do that' — when either option is fine: 주말에 자거나 영화를 봐요 ('on weekends I sleep or watch a movie'). The crucial split for English speakers is that Korean splits 'or' by part of speech: -거나 joins verbs/adjectives, while (이)나 joins nouns. So 'coffee or tea' (two nouns) is 커피나 차, but 'drink coffee or drink tea' (two verbs) is 커피를 마시거나 차를 마셔요. A second rival is -든지, which adds a 'whichever, no matter which' nuance ('do whatever, sleep or watch a movie, I don't care'), while plain -거나 just lists open options neutrally. You can chain more than two: 자거나 먹거나 쉬어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 거나 to connect nouns (커피거나 차 is wrong — use 커피나 차) and confusing it with 아니면 ('or else / otherwise'), which links whole sentences rather than gluing two verbs inside one clause.
usage: On weekends I sleep or watch movies.
two verb actions offered as choices
I drink coffee or drink tea.
both verbs keep their own object
I take the bus or walk.
When bored I read or listen to music.
chains naturally after a 면 clause
examples: When tired, I rest or take a walk.
mistakes: Using 거나 to join nouns: 커피거나 차. For two nouns use (이)나 — 커피나 차 ('coffee or tea'). 거나 is only for verb/adjective stems.
Confusing it with 아니면. 아니면 links full clauses ('do A, or else B'): 지금 가거나 — to say 'go now, or else stay' you'd add 아니면: 지금 가, 아니면 여기 있어. Bare 거나 just lists options inside one clause.
Adding tense inside: 잤거나 봤어요 for a habitual 'I sleep or watch'. Keep the stem bare — 자거나 봐요 — and let the final verb carry tense.

formNote: 마다 is a particle you stick onto a noun to mean 'each / every one without exception', and it carries two flavors: with a time noun it means 'every time' (아침마다 = 'every morning'), and with a countable noun it means 'each individual one' (사람마다 = 'each person'). It often pairs with 다르다 to say things differ case by case: 나라마다 문화가 달라요 ('every country has a different culture'). Compare it with the standalone 매 (every) and 모든 (all): 매일 and 날마다 both mean 'every day', but 매 attaches to specific time words (매일, 매주, 매년) while 마다 is freer and can ride any noun (가게마다, 집집마다). And 모든 사람 ('all people') views the group as a whole, whereas 사람마다 zooms in on each member one by one. The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 마다 to a verb (자마다 is wrong) — for 'every time you do X' you need V(으)ㄹ 때마다 (잘 때마다) — and reaching for 매 with nouns it doesn't take, where 마다 is the safe, productive choice.
usage: Every country has a different culture.
examples: Prices differ from store to store.
I go to Busan every year.
mistakes: Attaching 마다 to a verb stem: 자마다 for 'every time I sleep'. Use V(으)ㄹ 때마다 instead — 잘 때마다 잠꼬대해요 ('I talk in my sleep every time I sleep').
Saying 매 사람 or 매 나라 with a 마다-type noun. 매 only pairs with set time words (매일, 매주); for 'each person/country' use 사람마다, 나라마다.
Confusing 사람마다 with 모든 사람. 모든 사람 treats everyone as one group ('all people'); 사람마다 stresses each person separately, usually to point out that they differ.

formNote: -자마자 fuses onto a verb stem to say the second action follows the first with zero gap: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요 ('the moment I get home, I wash my hands'). It is the tightest 'right after' connector. Compare it with V은/ㄴ 후에 ('after'), which only says B happens later, allowing any delay, while 자마자 insists on immediacy and often a touch of surprise — 도착한 후에 전화해요 = 'I'll call sometime after arriving', but 도착하자마자 전화해요 = 'I'll call the instant I arrive'. Two grammar facts trip learners up: never put a tense marker before 자마자 (write 끝나자마자, not 끝났자마자) even when the whole sentence is past, because the final verb carries the tense — 보자마자 웃었어요 ('I laughed the moment I saw it'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'as soon as' clauses that take their own tense in English ('as soon as I arrived'), and confusing it with the time noun phrase V는 대로, which is more formal and planning-oriented ('as soon as it's done, per arrangement').
usage: The moment I get home, I wash my hands.
B follows A with no gap at all
Right after I wake up, I drink water.
The instant class ends, I go home.
I slept the moment I finished eating.
tense (잤) sits only on the last verb
examples: I'll call as soon as I arrive.
I laughed the moment I heard it.
immediate reaction, past tense on 웃었어요
I fell for them at first sight, the instant I saw them.
mistakes: Putting tense before 자마자: 끝났자마자. The stem stays plain — 끝나자마자 — and the final verb shows tense (끝나자마자 갔어요).
Using V은 후에 when you mean immediacy. 도착한 후에 전화해요 allows a delay ('after arriving, at some point'); for 'the instant I arrive' you need 도착하자마자 전화해요.
Treating it as two separate sentences and re-stating the subject. 자마자 binds one tight clause; do not say 제가 오자마자 제가 씻어요 — drop the repeated subject: (저는) 오자마자 씻어요.

formNote: V(으)려면 is a contraction of 려고 하면 ('if you intend/plan to'), so it sets up a goal and then states what you must do to reach it: 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요 ('if you mean to get good at Korean, practice daily'). Use 려면 after a vowel-final stem (가려면, 잘하려면) and 으려면 after a consonant-final stem (읽으려면, 먹으려면). It naturally leads into advice or requirements, so it loves to pair with 야 하다/돼요, 세요, or 필요하다: 건강하려면 잘 자야 해요. Contrast it with the plain conditional -(으)면, which states a neutral 'if/when' about facts, while -(으)려면 specifically frames a deliberate goal or intention you are aiming at: 비가 오면 = 'if it rains' (a circumstance), but 살을 빼려면 = 'if you intend to lose weight' (your aim). The English-speaker pitfalls are dropping the 으 on consonant stems (읽려면 is wrong — say 읽으려면) and using 려면 for things outside your control; since it implies intention, you would not say 비가 오려면 for 'if it rains', because rain is not something you intend.
usage: To get good at Korean, practice daily.
잘하- ends in a vowel, so plain 려면
If you want to be healthy, you must sleep well.
읽- is a consonant stem, so 으려면
If you mean to catch the train, hurry.
goal first, then the necessary step
examples: If you want to lose weight, exercise.
naturally pairs with the 세요 command
To succeed, you have to put in effort.
goal → required condition with 야 해요
To buy a house, you must save money.
intention plus the practical step to get there
mistakes: Dropping the 으 after a consonant stem: 읽려면, 먹려면. Consonant stems need it — 읽으려면, 먹으려면.
Using 려면 for uncontrollable events: 비가 오려면 for 'if it rains'. 려면 implies intention, and rain is not intended, so use the plain conditional 비가 오면.
Confusing it with neutral -(으)면. 가면 = 'if/when you go' (a condition); 가려면 = 'if you intend to go (then do X)'. Use 려면 only when a deliberate goal is in view.
